utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honour, counsel and everyone around and in the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for Defence counsel. They have a new team today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President; good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant; and Alexis Demirdjian, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I greet everyone present at this hearing in November, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused and everyone else in the courtroom, including the interpreters who on Friday were working a little longer. Mr. Registrar, I think we have to deal with certain documents that will be tendered into evidence. Could we have the numbers for these documents, please. Yes, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, given that on Thursday we worked intensively, it wasn't possible for Defence counsel to suggest which documents should be admitted into evidence, I'd like to do that now with your leave. Halim Husic was shown eight documents, which are contained in our exhibit list, and he was shown three documents which are on the list of exhibits that have already been admitted in this case. Out of the eight documents, some of these documents were drafted by the witness himself. As far as the other ones are concerned, he is familiar with the events referred to in those documents as he witnessed then, and some of the documents were documents that he recognised given the facts he was acquainted with in 1992 and 1993. As a result, Defence counsel suggests that 0528 be admitted into evidence as well as the following documents, 0572, 0588, 0915, 0918, 1010, 1043, and 1368. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give the floor to the Prosecution now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The documents will be admitted under the following numbers DH528, and its English version will be DH581/E; DH572, the English version will be DH572/E; DH588, its English version is DH588/E; DH915, the English version will be DH915/E; DH918, the English version will be DH918/E. DH1010, the English version will be DH1010/E; DH1043, the English version will be DH1043/E; and finally DH1368, the English version will be DH1368/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar, we have taken note of these eight documents that have been admitted into evidence under the numbers that you have just mentioned. If there are no other documents to be tendered into evidence, we'll now call the expert witness into the courtroom so that he can take the solemn declaration. Mr. Usher, could you call the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to be sure that you can hear what I'm saying in your own language. If so, please say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've heard your answer, but I did not receive the interpretation. Could you please repeat what you just said. Could you tell me whether you heard me in your own language or not. For the moment, I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I heard what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called here as a witness for the Defence. Before you take the solemn declaration, I would be grateful if you could tell me your first and last names, your date of birth and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Zijad Sehic. I'm -- I lecture in the contemporary history at the university in Sarajevo. I lecture in the general history of the new century and in modern history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 23rd of October, 1959, in Mrkonjic Grad in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified before an international or national court as an expert witness or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This will be the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now ask the usher to show the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, before Defence commences with its examination-in-chief with regard to your expert report that we have all received, there is some information I would like to provide you with to enable you to answer the questions put to you by the Defence and the Prosecution to the best of your ability as well as in order to enable you to answer the Judges' questions. You have been called here as an expert witness. The Defence asked you to write a report on the historical background in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in this way to provide the Judges with information on the history of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the events that occurred from 1990 to 1995. In order to do this, you have provided us with a report with numerous annexes. In the course of this procedure which is based on the common law system, you will have to answer the questions that will be put to you by the Defence with regard to the contents of your expert report. In the course of its cross-examination, the Prosecution may also ask you questions about your report, and the three Judges who are sitting before you, if they deem this necessary, may ask you questions. You are an expert witness; you are not a factual witness. You have been called to testify here as an historian. You've taken the solemn declaration, which means that you should speak the truth, and you should answer the questions put to you to the best of your ability. Naturally, experts do not lie. That goes without saying. But you should be aware if the Trial Chamber believes that false testimony is given, this could be punished. This is how we will be proceeding. Try to answer the questions put to you by the Defence to the best of your ability. In any event, we do have your written report, which will make it easier for us to follow your answers. The objective is to provide us with clarifications on the background in that region, the historical, economic, political, and social Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond background in Bosnia and Herzegovina. If you encounter any difficulties when questions are put to you, please inform us of the fact. We will try to solve any problems to the extent that this is possible. So roughly speaking, this is how we will be proceeding in the course of the hearing today, and your testimony should take up the entire hearing. I will now give the floor to the Defence, who will commence with their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Sehic.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the Trial Chamber has provided you with detailed information about how we will be examining you, but before I start asking you a series of questions, I would also like that point out the following: As we speak the same language, you might attempt to immediately answer my questions. However, I would be grateful if you could pause after my question so that the interpreters can interpret my question, and so that my colleagues and the Chamber can follow what is being said. Have you understood me, Mr. Sehic?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sehic, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, could you provide us with details from your bibliography and could you tell us about your professional qualifications?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 23rd of October, 1959 in Mrkonjic Grad in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is where I completed primary and secondary school. I enrolled in the faculty of philosophy, the history department, in 1978, and I graduated in 1982. After I had served in the military, I enrolled to pursue post-graduate studies which I completed in 1991. I obtained my masters with a master thesis called "The annexation crisis from 1908 to 1909, in the light of European historiography.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what current academic qualifications you have?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: I currently work at the philosophy faculty in Sarajevo. I lecture in the general history of the new century, and modern history.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to your duties at the university, in the course of your professional work as a doctor in history, were you ever engaged in other spheres or did you hold other public positions that were related to your professional expertise?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was involved in a number of projects. These projects have been completed now. One of them was part of a larger project. I was the representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina in a large-scale project, south-east Europe as part of European history, and this was under the supervision of Dr. Holm Sundhausen from the Free University in Vienna. In addition, I've also participated in number of other projects. Currently I'm a member of the state commission for writing textbooks on history. As far as my other duties are concerned, I'm involved in professional work, in scientific work, so I have published certain other academic works.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, have you published any books, any textbooks or any professional studies? And if that is the case, where?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: As far as my academic work is concerned, my academic opus is concerned, I have published one book together with Dr. Ibrahim Tepic. It's a historical atlas of Bosnia and Herzegovina; Bosnia and Herzegovina on geographic and historical maps. This was published in 2002. This book has been translated into English and German. It will soon be published. In addition to that I'm the author of about 30 academic studies papers. I'm also the author of seven textbooks in history. These are textbooks for primary and secondary schools.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sehic, would it be correct to say that in the last 15 years you have been mainly involved in the history of Bosnia and Herzegovina in a professional sense?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that would be correct. And it's been a little over 15 years perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Dr. Sehic, could you now tell me how it is that you wrote the report that we will be discussing today before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: I think that at the beginning of October, I contacted Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic and for Mr. Kubura, and after having been informed of what this report should consist of, I agreed to write it, but at the time I had a scholarship and I was studying in Germany, and I thought that after completing my studies in Germany, I would get involved in writing this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was Defence counsel's main request apart from the fact that they asked you whether as a professional or given your professional duties, apart from being asked whether you could execute this task?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: The main task that I was given had to do with portraying international diplomacy and its effect on the political events in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the course of 1992 and 1993, but the scope was subsequently widened, and it was also necessary to address other issues. For example, the relation between the Bosnian and Herzegovinian population with regard to its cultural heritage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, in addition to these two specific issues, was the subject of your expert report also the general historical background that had an effect on the situation and the current position in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was also the main task when I was requested to draft this report. It was necessary to describe the historical background in relation to the events referred to in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, could you now tell the Trial Chamber about the sources and the material that you used when drafting your report?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Since I was -- I have been involved in the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina for a long time and I have spent a significant amount of time in Germany, I used various kinds of literature. I had access to such literature, and I analysed this literature from 1992 onwards. As for other aspects that are important if one wants to analyse historical issues or the historical background to the events that we are concerned with, these aspects involved my investigation into Yugoslavia. They involved participation in academic conferences. And as I had a number of scholarships and was able to study abroad on a number of occasions, I could examine, within the European context, what had been done with regard to this subject. I was in a position to examine the relevant literature. The Defence counsel provided me with archival material, above all from the BH army and from the HVO. Also material from other case before this Tribunal. For example, the Celebici, Blaskic, Kordic cases. So I had a lot of material, a lot of literature I could refer to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, what method or what was your methodology when drafting your expert report?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: When I was working on my expert report, the methodology I followed was the one that any historian would follow. This had to do with examining material from various sources. In addition, I used -- apart from using material from various sources, it's necessary to point out that you need to follow a comparative methodology. You have to compare the material from various sources, and you have to check or verify certain information, certain facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sehic, as an historian, are there any problems when it is necessary to assess events that took place in the recent past?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: For any historian, there are certain number of problems because of so-called theory of historical distance. If one is to provide conclusions about historical events in recent past, this is very difficult. One often falls into certain traps, and one is thus unable to be objective or to examine the matter from a number of viewpoints. It is only once there is a certain historical distance, it is only after the passage of time that one can provide the relevant conclusions in a more objective manner. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you analysed the Austro-Hungarian period, and you mentioned the subject you now lecture in at the university. Since part of your expert report also dealt with part of the history of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, could you tell us whether when drafting this report you consulted any other individuals or were you assisted by anyone else?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Since this is not my strict field of academic interest and since this is an important part of my expert report, I also consulted experts from this area. Above all, I consulted Dr. Mustafa Imamovic who works at the school of law in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sehic, could you tell us which subject Mr. -- Dr. Mustafa Imamovic lectures in?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Well, he lectures in the history of states and in law.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see that you have the report before you. Could you now tell us whether this is the report that you drafted in the manner that you have already described, and is this the report that you provided Defence counsel with?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the report in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you divided this report, how you broke it down when drafting it?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: This report consists of an introduction and seven parts. In the introduction, we have general information about the Central Bosnian area, and seven other parts indicated on the title page, from A to G. Under A, we deal with the historical development of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the 10th century to 1980. Under B, the report deals with the main processes in dissolution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia from 1980 to 1991. The third part deals with political events in Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1990 up until 1992. The fourth part, under D, deals with military and political developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina from international recognition on the 6th -- or, rather, the 7th of April, 1992, and until the end of that year. In the fifth part, under letter E, the subject dealt with is Bosnia and Herzegovina and international diplomacy in the course of 1993. And it also describes the political developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina in that year. The sixth part, under F, deals with Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1994. And under G, the political relations in Central Bosnia in 1994 and in 1993 are described.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, next to you I can see three binders. Can you please tell us what these binders are all about, and did you hand over these binders together with your expert report to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes. These three binders are archives, literature, and references which were used while I was drafting my report. The footnotes in the historical report can be found in the documents contained within these three binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sehic, in addition to having drafted the report and in addition to having handed over the relevant documents to the Defence team, the documents that accompany your report, the report, did you also draft another document, and did you hand it over together with your expert report?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: In addition to the expert report, I also handed over a set containing a total of 17 historical maps. My objective was to illustrate the expert report and to explain it better by providing additional information based on these maps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what the source was for compiling this set of maps that you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: In order to compile this set of maps, I used several sources. I myself am the author of the historical atlas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and most of these maps can be found within that atlas. I also used some other maps, the maps that were used in the Celebici case. I also used a set of maps published by Professor Kasim Begic to cover the period after the year 1992. It was published in his book "Bosnia-Herzegovina from Vance-Owen Plan to Dayton."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to give the witness the original set of maps. The registry has photocopied this set for us and they can be found at the end of all the documents. This is to be done for the witness to recognise this set as his own documents and to be able to use this set while answering my questions. The original has been handed over together with our submission to the Trial Chamber so the original document can also be found at the registry. We all have coloured photocopied -- photocopies of all the 17 documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, is this the document that you drafted?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document that I drafted, a total of 17 maps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would kindly ask you to go to page 5 of your expert report. And this is also page 5 of the English translation of your report. Can you please tell me, what is the period from which date the reliable data on Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what was its status up to the 15th century? At the same time, I would kindly ask you to illustrate your words by showing it on map number 1. Since we all have this map, maybe it wouldn't be a bad idea to have it put on the ELMO at the same time. I don't know whether the whole map can be displayed on the ELMO because the scale is 1:3. Thank you. I think this will suffice. Can you please answer my question, Dr. Sehic.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: The first reliable data on Bosnia-Herzegovina go back to mid-10th century, the Byzantine emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus, in his document called "De Administrando Imperio," in other words, the administration of the Empire, mentions Bosnia -- Bosnia, that is, for the first time as a small state, horion Bosona, with two towns, Katera and Desnek.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The map that you have in front of you, what is it?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: The map that we have in front of us depicts several historical maps that encompass the period of the medieval ages. First and foremost, the first map that we can see now --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you point on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: The first map that we can see is the map of the original Bosnia in the 10th century. The second map, the second part of it, depicts Bosnia and Herzegovina during the period of the reign of Ban Kulin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please point to those lines on the ELMO, otherwise we won't be able to follow your words.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: This is the line. This is the territory. And the third territory is the territory that existed during the reign of Stjepan Kotromanic. This is Bosnia from that period of time. And the fourth territory that you can see here is Bosnia and Herzegovina during the reign of King Tvrtko. And this is the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the 14th century when Bosnia and Herzegovina was at its peak, when it was the biggest. In 1377 Bosnia-Herzegovina became a kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sehic, can you please tell us what is represented by the thick line on this map? It shows some borders, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: This line represents the current borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is the green line that you can see on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Sehic, can you please tell us now what changes occurred in the territory of the Balkan Peninsula and Bosnia-Herzegovina in mid-15th century, and what was the status of Bosnia and Herzegovina after these developments and changes? As you are giving us your answer, can you please use the next map.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Significant changes in this area happened towards the end of the 14th century after the battle on the field of Kosovo. In the south-eastern Europe, the Osman Empire became a very important creator of the politics in this part of Europe and especially in the Balkan Peninsula. For Bosnia, these developments will have a major impact since the Osman Empire appeared in Bosnia in the 30s of the 15th century in the parish of Vrhbosna where they built their first strongholds. This will continue until the year 1463 when Bosnia fell under the Osman rule. From the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- or Bosnia, rather, there's a further onslaught of Turks and the plan was to advance towards central Europe. In the territory of Bosnia, an administrative unit was established as well as the forces that would be capable of advancing further and enlarging the Turkish Empire. In 1570, the Bosnian eyalet was established. It was also called the Bosnian pashalik. According to this map that you can see here, you can see where the borders of the Bosnian eyalet were in the year 1570. You can also see that its northern borders were in the area of today's Slavonija all the way up to Virovitica, and that the territory of Bosnia was much larger than territory of the medieval Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Sehic. Kindly look at page 6 of your report, the last three sentences in the Bosnian original or in the English version, page 3, the last nine lines in the third paragraph. Can you please explain what principle of life was applied in Bosnia and Herzegovina for centuries?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: The mixing of population in the territory of Bosnia caused the birth of such a society which in modern time is called a multi-ethnic society. There was a mosaic of population which involved the Sephardic Jews who came to this territory in mid-16th century. Let me draw a parallel with the religious communities in Europe. It is well known that this was the period of religious war and that the general principle which prevailed in Europe was Cuius regio, eius religio. Bosnia for the most part or the Bosnian eyalet departed from this principle. Proof of that can also be the fact that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the territory that covers one square kilometre, you could find the religious buildings of all the main monotheistic religions. In the territory of one square kilometre in Sarajevo, you can find a Jewish synagogue, an Islamic mosque, a Catholic church, an Orthodox church, a Protestant church as well. So Bosnia departed from the general principle that prevailed in Europe at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, can you please now tell us how the borders of the so-called Bosnian eyalet, throughout centuries and especially in the 18th and 19th century changed, and when was it that they assumed the shape that Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state has today?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: The forming of the border of the modern Bosnia-Herzegovina is a very dynamic process which is very hard to follow in all of its details. Towards the end of the 17th century, the Karlovac peace treaty established borders on the River Sava. There were a number international agreements which registered a situation after various wars. In the same fashion, the borders of the state of Bosnia was -- was registered. The first one was the Peace Treaty of Carlowitz, then the Treaty of Possarowitz in 1718, then the Belgrade Treaty in 1739 and Sistova Treaty in 1791. All of these changes which took place in the 18th century were registered by the Vienna Congress which took place in 19 -- in 1814 and -- 1814 and 1815. This Congress made some change -- some decisions implicitly recognising the borders of the Osman Empire and sultan as the superior ruler of the Balkan Peninsula, and implicitly this is how the borders of Bosnia were recognised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sehic, I would now kindly ask you to go to another historical period, and this period was described by yourself on pages 7 and 8 or the English page 7. Can you please tell us about the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the reign of Austro-Hungarian Empire?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: When Bosnia-Herzegovina was occupied in 1878, after 415 years Bosnia abandoned the Islamic influence and adapted itself to the Western influences. As far as the legal position of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the Austro-Hungarian administration from 1878 to 1918, there would be several stages. Bosnia was occupied in 1878, and this is the situation that would remain until the year 1908 when Bosnia was annexed. And it was finally annexed to the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Until that year, the sultan was still the supreme commander or the supreme ruler. Some significant changes, despite of what was happening, despite the annexation, some significant changes did not take place in the state itself. Its legal position remained the same. Bosnia and Herzegovina did not belong either to the Austrian or to Hungarian part of the monarchy. It was perceived as a separate part of this Empire. That's why the inhabitants of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not have the nationality of either Austria or Hungarian. They enjoyed a specific status. They were considered members of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since the witness has provided us with a number of documents, the Defence does not intend to show all of these documents to the witness. That is why we have made a compilation for the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution. I would like to show the witness this compilation. And we have marked these documents with our numbers from our document list. This will help us later on when we tender all of these documents for admission. We are going to be using the numbers that are already on our list. I would now kindly ask the usher to help us with showing this compilation to the witness and to our learned friends and the Trial Chamber. We have actually already provided the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber with the compilation of documents that Dr. Sehic has provided us with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sehic, in the first section are documents from your annex A. I would just like you to confirm that the first document is an excerpt from the historical atlas of Bosnia-Herzegovina which you wrote.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The second document, could you tell us what it is, please, and whether that has anything to do with the position of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the Austro-Hungarian administration. That is document number 03500, and it was in your annex under number 4.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: This is the land constitution for Bosnia and Herzegovina for 1910. In order to regulate the legal status of Bosnia and Herzegovina, this land constitution was declared, or the statute, as it was called, for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you, Dr. Sehic, to tell us, please, what changes were brought to Bosnia and Herzegovina with World War I, and if you can explain to us what we can see on map number 3.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: World War I brought great sorrow and suffering and destruction to the South Slav peoples, but it also brought on the possibility of creating a common state. The main supporters of this unification were the Serbian government and the Yugoslav committee. Already in the course of the war, you could sense the future concept of the resolution of the Yugoslav question. On one side there was the concept that the regions which were under Austro-Hungarian administration, a third body be formed within the monarchy which was provided for in case the central axis forces won. On the other hand, there was a different solution in case the entente powers won. Significant changes came about in 1918, especially towards the end of the war. In October, this third body, entity was formed which comprised the property, the lands or the territory which had been under the Austro-Hungarian administration. Since the end of the war was close and since the 14 points declared by US President Wilson on the rights of nations and peoples and states to self-determination had already been published, the Croatian council severed its legal connections with Hungary, and after that a state of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes was formed, a state which comprised the areas which had formerly been under Austro-Hungarian administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sehic, does that mean that Bosnia and Herzegovina in its entirety entered this state?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes. It became a part of this state in its entirety, which would exist for the next two months until the 1st of December, the decree of December 1st, which created the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. Bosnia-Herzegovina, in any case, in the state of Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs, had its own representatives, its people's assembly or council and its bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to ask you to tell us what went on in the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, and what position did Bosnia and Herzegovina have in this kingdom, especially from the aspect of the protection of its historical territories?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: In this euphoric moment in 1918, it seemed as if finally the South Slavs had united. At the end of 1918, the Austro-Hungarian monarchy broke apart, and on the ruins of that kingdom and the newly established country of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, this Kingdom of Serb, Croats, and Slovenes was formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at map 4 and explain to us what we can see there?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: This is the formation about -- of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes on 1st of December, 1918. And you can see, especially regarding the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that it was still a separate territorial entity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please now look at document in your annex A which has number 0351. The constitution of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. And can you tell us whether there was a guarantee there for the preservation of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the St. Vitus Day constitution adopted on the 28th of June, 1921. Thanks to the fact that the Yugoslav Muslim organisation managed to work for the preservation of the territorial integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So Article 135 of the St. Vitus constitution provided for the okrugs from the periods of the Austro-Hungarian monarchy become districts. After that, Bosnia-Herzegovina preserved its territorial integrity, which it enjoyed also during the period of the Austro-Hungarian rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you, Dr. Sehic, to move to the part of your findings on pages 11 to 14. In the English text it's from page 9 to 12. And if you could explain to us which events between the two world wars had a significant influence on the position of Bosnia and Herzegovina and also a more far-reaching effect on events in the -- which have just passed.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: The creation of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes in itself was burdened -- created a burden for the political relations within the country. These political relations will culminate in 1928 with the killing in the national assembly. The way out or solution from this situation was sought by King Aleksandar, who on the 6th of January, 1929 declared a dictatorship, he imposed a dictatorship, an effect of which was a centralisation of the state and which led to administrative territorial divisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We see now on the screen image 05. Could you please tell us what that is and what it means for the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which as we could see on earlier maps was -- had maintained its territorial integrity throughout history.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: This map shows the administrative territorial divisions of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia under the law on the administrative territorial divisions dating from the 3rd of October, whereby the country was divided into nine banovinas and the country was renamed Yugoslavia. On this map, when Bosnia-Herzegovina is looked at, you can see its entire territorial decomposition. Why? The reason for that was that its historical territories were divided amongst five banovina areas. For the first time -- for a long time in its history, Bosnia and Herzegovina goes through complete territorial disintegration or decomposition, and this will stay in force all -- until 1939. The relationships amongst the parties in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia were deteriorating. These were the relationships between Serbs and Croats also, and they were leading towards a final solution of the Croatian question. After 1929, or after the introduction of the dictatorship or the imposition of the dictatorship, this relationship deteriorated to a great degree which culminated after 1935, and this will then bring in a period in which new solutions were being sought as reflected by the threat of the fascist forces, Germany and Italy, which would force the ruling powers from Belgrade to find a solution in reaching an agreement with the Croats. This agreement was signed in August 1939, and it will establish the banovina of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, could you point out on the map all these things that you are talking about. On map 06 could you please tell us how this was done and what the effects of this were for Bosnia and Herzegovina in that period, and also in the immediate past, the recent past.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: You can see this division from 1939 on this map. If we look at this map, the areas in green show the territory of the banovina of Croatia, and the rest of the territory is the territory of the other of the banovina areas which are not part of the banovina of Croatia, after which there was a project or a concept which emerged of Serbian countries. So everything that was outside of the boundaries of the banovina of Croatia was supposed to be united with -- with the capital in Skopje in Macedonia, and these were to be Serbian lands.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please show us this on the map. Is this the map of the Serbian countries that you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is that area that was supposed to make up the rest of the territory which was outside of the banovina of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sehic, were there forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina which were opposed to this division of their ancient territory?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: In this period following the Cvetkovic-Macek agreement and the forming of the Croatian banovina in 1939 in Bosnia-Herzegovina itself there were some changes. This way of conducting policies and maintaining mutual relations created the need to begin a struggle for the autonomy of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which meant that the Muslim population was looking for a way out of the situation the way it was in acquiring autonomy for Bosnia and Herzegovina, which culminated at the end of December in 1939. All these divisions had a significant effect on future developments, because they would start numerous debates about who Bosnia actually belonged to, which would then culminate in war in 1941. All these plans on the division of the country and the redistribution of its territory to a large extent contributed to the events which occurred after the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, I would now like to look -- you to look at map 08 and tell us what was happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina in World War II. Which forces once again restored the historical territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and restored its equal position in relation to the others?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: On map number 8, you can see the division of Yugoslavia following the occupation in 1941. What can we see here? Yellow indicates the Independent State of Croatia, which was formed in Zagreb in 1941. And the other parts which were parts of different sectors and belonged to different forces, collaborationist forces --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think that there is no need for you to go into any detail for that period, but you can just tell us whether this was a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was exposed to a lot of suffering, especially as a result of the active -- activities of the fascist forces of Italy and Germany.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: After the occupation of Yugoslavia and its division into spheres of interest and the establishment of demarcation lines which ran throughout the territory of Yugoslavia, quisling systems were also set up. They were different types. Their objectives were different, but their common goal was that they participated in the organisation of the occupying power's authority. These quisling systems I've already said in Zagreb on the 10th of April, the Independent State of Croatia was established. This was the Ustasha movement. And in the territory of Serbia, the Chetnik movement came to the fore. All these coalition forces or all these systems participated in the ruling structures of Italy and Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was their attitude towards the Bosniak Muslim population and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: After 1941, after October 1941, Bosnia became a part of the Independent State of Croatia. The name of Bosnia and Herzegovina could no longer be publicly mentioned in the media, in public speeches. After the Independent State of Croatia was established, a part of the Bosniak population joined that power while the rest remained in opposition to it. A large number of people, the intelligentsia primarily, business people, the clergy were opposed to the Ustasha authorities and the Independent State of Croatia. The result of that were the well-known anti-Ustasha resolutions which were adopted after 1941 in different towns in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As part of this bundle of documents, could you please look at document under number 4. I'm talking about the bundle of documents. And could you please tell us whether these are resolutions which you have just now mentioned and which were a form of resistance to the Ustasha terror and resistance of -- towards or opposition to Muslims who participated amongst the ranks of Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes, these were such resolutions. They were adopted in a number of towns in Bosnia. And as you can see, one such resolution was translated into English. This is the resolution adopted in the town of Mostar, but the other adopted resolutions were more or less the same. And the essence was that they condemned the crimes that were committed. They condemned the crimes committed by the Ustashas. They did not back those crimes, and they condemned Muslims who had participated in such acts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sehic, I have an additional part within this question. What was the Independent State of Croatia's attitude towards the Muslim nation? Did they recognise them as a separate and distinct people, and whatever the attitude of the Chetnik movement in relation to that part of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: As far as the attitude of these forces towards Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Muslims is concerned and in particular towards the population, as I have already said, some of the inhabitants were parts of the Ustasha movement but others were part of the resistance movement. But the Ustasha believed that all Croats would live in the territory of the NDH, the Independent State of Croatia. And the Muslims who for nationalist reasons had been declared as the flower of Croathood. On the other hand, with regard to the Muslims, other collaborationist forces had a different attitude. For example, the Chetniks. The numerous crimes committed in the course of 1941 and 1942 also had an influence on a change of attitude on the part of the Muslims, the Croats, and the Serbs. If in 1941 there was a revolt led by the communist leadership of Yugoslavia, these crimes contributed to an extent to diminish the force of the collaborationist forces and to strengthen the force of the partisans.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, could you please have a look at map number 10 and tell me what it represents, or, rather, within the anti-fascist movement, what was the position of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: This map represents the idea of creating a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm now looking at the map that we commented on a minute ago. This is a map of Serbia and NDH, the Independent State of Croatia, but I wanted you to have a look at map number 10. We're talking about the anti-fascist movement and the position of Bosnia and Herzegovina in relation to this movement, in relation to the first session of ZAVNOBiH, the Anti-fascist Council of People's Liberation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the first session of AVNOJ, the Anti-fascist Council of People's Liberation of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: At the same time that they were fighting again the occupier in the country in 1941 and 1942, the construction of people's power commenced. In various parts of the country, they started forming anti-fascist councils of people's liberation. Such a council for Bosnia-Herzegovina was formed between the 25th and 26th of November, 1943 in Mrkonjic Grad. What's the importance of this council and the resolution? Above all, the result of the war was that certain results obtained were legalised and resolution of the Anti-fascist Council of People's Liberation confirmed the creation of the statehood of Bosnia-Herzegovina and confirmed the idea of re-establishing Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state. This decision was late supplemented or, rather, confirmed at the second session of the Anti-fascist Council of People's Liberation of Yugoslavia in 1943 in Jajce. This process of creating a state in Bosnia and Herzegovina was continued in 1944 with the second session of ZAVNOBiH, the Anti-fascist Council of People's Liberation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And this ZAVNOBiH was supposed to become a legitimate state organ. And in April, 1945, at the third session, this was also done in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, the declaration resolutions of ZAVNOBiH, and AVNOJ, how did they regulate the issue of peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Who did Bosnia-Herzegovina belong to?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: In the resolution, it is stated that Bosnia and Herzegovina is neither Serbian nor Croatian nor Muslim. It is both Serbian and Croatian and Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could we have a look at the document under A14 now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, Mrs. Residovic, it's half past three. It would be best to have our break now, and we will resume at about 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sehic, could you please have a look in the bundle of documents, the ones under annex A, 5, 6, and 7. That is at the end of annex A. And could you tell me what are these documents that represent the resolutions of ZAVNOBiH and AVNOJ, about which you have just testified and in which it is just stated that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be an equal state within the SFRY, the Federative Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes. These documents refer to the creation of Bosnia and Herzegovina or, rather, to its status, organisation as a state. These are the resolutions from the first session of ZAVNOBiH, from the second session of ZAVNOBiH, as well as from the third session. One should also mention the AVNOJ resolution. And these resolutions were adopted at the first session of ZAVNOBiH in Mrkonjic Grad. They were made legally valid at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Sehic. Could we now have a look at the part of your report that concerns -- on page 23 and page 30, or, rather, in English -- in the English report it's between page 19 and 25. And tell me, with regard to the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, what sort of events were there that heralded the break-up of Yugoslavia, and could you tell me about the consequences of the events in 1991 and 1992 for Bosnia and Herzegovina. What were the consequences of these events for Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: The crucial event that had an influence on all the events that occurred from 1980 until 1992 was the death of Josip Broz Tito, a charismatic figure and a key person from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. One could say that with the death of Tito, a certain phase in Yugoslavia's history came to an end, a phase that could be -- that one could describe as a peaceful one. There were significant changes in 1980 in that individual Yugoslav republics were placed within the historical framework. According to the 1974 constitution, all Yugoslav republics were granted to a certain extent the character of statehood. The general social crisis which occurred in Yugoslavia after 1980, which was evident in the economy, in rampant inflation, was evident in the fact that the standard of living was that of the 1960s. These factors had a significant influence on the subsequent stage. This general social crisis accompanied by a breakdown of the governing ideology resulted in, one could say, after a 40-year taboo period, resulted in a creation of the conditions for the appearance of nationalist forces, and the ground was extremely fertile for such forces. The centre of this -- these nationalistic disturbances was not in the periphery of Yugoslavia but in the core of Yugoslavia, in Serbia. So one could say that this eruption resulted in the break-up of the entire Yugoslav construction. Two important documents heralded this new nationalist ideology. There were two petitions -- or, rather, the first one was from 1986, and it concerned an expulsion of -- or the prosecution of Serbs in Kosovo. And then there was the memorandum of the Serbian academy of arts and science, and these documents one could say established the groundwork for a nationalist type of politics. What one should also point out is that the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Arts And Science from 1986 established the groundworks for this ideology and it consisted of three main objectives. The first one was the homogenisation of peoples, the second was the centralisation of Serbia, and the third one was carrying through the idea of Greater Serbia. The practical implementation of this political idea commenced after 1987 with the arrival of Slobodan Milosevic on the political scene. He, above all, tried to take advantage of the Kosovo problem and put oil on the fire, and by expressing his solidarity with the Serbs in Kosovo he established such a route in the main institutions. In order to centralise Serbia it was necessary to revoke the autonomy of Vojvodina and Kosovo, two autonomous provinces which according to the constitution from 1974 were no longer under the control of Belgrade. Tito had granted autonomy to Vojvodina and Kosovo. In the 1986 memorandum, it is also said that Serbia doesn't have control over its own territory, and for this reason it was necessary to deprive Kosovo and Vojvodina of their autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, I don't want to go into the details of those occurrences in Serbia, but could you now tell me how those events had an influence or affected other parts of Yugoslavia? What sort of movements were there in the other republics, and at sometime in 1991, were there any armed conflicts? Did war break out?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: There were two diametrically opposed concepts. One was a federal one, and the other was a confederal one which was favoured by Slovenia and Croatia above all. The agreements that were reached in the course of 1989 and 1990 exacerbated these positions. So when -- it was impossible to agree on the concept of a state that would satisfy all the parties involved. Slovenia and Croatia decided to declare their independence in 1991. This is what they in fact did, and that is when the first war in the area of Yugoslavia broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The events in Slovenia and Croatia, did they have an effect on Bosnia and Herzegovina, and could you say whether the material and documents that you had provided you with a basis upon which you could come to the conclusion that they did have such an effect?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: All these events and the war in Slovenia and Croatia in 1991 had significant consequences for Bosnia and Herzegovina above all. After peace had been established in 1991 in Slovenia, all the military units that had previously been deployed in Slovenia were moved to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The main parts of the corps were moved to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and at the time they said that Bosnia and Herzegovina was the largest barracks in the world. In -- as far as policy -- policies are concerned, there was significant changes. Serbian autonomous regions were formed, and they continued to proclaim such regions, the existence of such regions in the course of 1991. Apart from declaring existence of such Serbian autonomous regions, the Croats also declared the existence of Croatian autonomous regions. So, these two ideas were present in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, did the international community take note of those problems, and did they respond to them in good time?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning one could say that the international community was not prepared for what happened in Yugoslavia, for what happened in the territory of Yugoslavia. It's a fact that all the countries, and in particular the main countries in world politics insisted that the Yugoslav federation should be preserved whatever the form of this federation. The material aid was also offered for Yugoslavia to become an integral part of European political processes, but one could say that it was impossible to do anything more than what was done. The international community reacted at -- at quite a late date, so it was only after the conflict in Slovenia and Croatia broke out that it issued a number of resolutions and became more actively involved in these events. A resolution was adopted according to which an embargo was to be imposed on delivering weapons to any area within the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, at that time when, as you said, various Serbian autonomous regions and various Croatian autonomous regions were created, at that time what was the structure of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and could you please answer this question with a reference to maps number 11 and 12.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: As far as the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina is concerned and its distribution, the last census took place in 1991. I would like to go back in time and look at the history of the whole thing. Over the past hundred years, to a large extent the distribution of the population in Bosnia and Herzegovina has been changed. The 1885 census showed that there were over 50 per cent of mixed settlements in Bosnia and Herzegovina. With time, the percentage decreased [as interpreted]. So according to the next census, the 1991 census, the number of mixed settlements in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was 80 out of 100. In 1991, it was often said that the distribution of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina reminded of a leopard skin. There were almost no ethnically uniform territories save for the territory of Western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These maps, maps number 11 and 12 with the official overview of the distribution of the population, do they reflect exactly what you have just told us?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes. This may be concluded from these two maps. This is the distribution of the population in 1991 and the participation in each of the peoples in the total population. And the second map depicts -- in the second map, however, you can see the majority population surpassing 50 per cent in particular areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Little while ago you told us that there were two opposing nationalist politics and that under their influence there was the creation of various so-called nationalist autonomous regions in Bosnia and Herzegovina and their character was primarily a nationalist one. Before I put a question to you, Mr. Sehic, with regard to the two maps that we have seen, was it at all possible to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina according to the national criteria or the ethnic criteria?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: If one were to carry out such a division according to the ethnic criteria, this could only be done by force, and this could only be done against all the principles of what was happening and what had been known in the history of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have also told us, Mr. Sehic, that the regionalisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and creation of autonomous regions was the result of certain desires of nationalist circles. At that time, did our neighbours discuss the issue of Bosnia-Herzegovina? What was their attitude towards the equality of that state with regard to the other republics of the former Yugoslavia? What was their idea? What did they want to leave to the most numerous population in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Can you please look at map 13 and use it for your answer if you're in the position to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: As far as this map is concerned, this depicts a nationalistic concept of Serbian autonomous regions. This is more or less this part of the territory, and this part of the territory on the right-hand side. The blue colour depicts the Croatian autonomous regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is the region that I'm talking about. Now, when you look at this map, what is without any colour, this was foreseen as the territory to be given to Muslims. So the territory for the most numerous people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and according to the 1991 census they made up 43 per cent of the total population, and they were given only 3.52 per cent of the whole territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Sehic, did there come a time when the international community started getting more seriously involved in the issue of the former Yugoslavia? What was the status or what opinions did they voice with regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: The international community started looking at this issue from October 1991. The issue became the top of the agenda in December. The Badinter Commission was established. Its president was the president of the French Constitutional Court, Mr. Badinter. On the 7th of December, 1991, this commission established that the -- when the Yugoslavian republic were being established, this was not a secession but a breakdown of the federal state of Yugoslavia. The European Community, on the 16th of February, 1991, provided all the details for the establishment of new states in the former Soviet Union and the former Yugoslavia, the states that would be established on democratic principles. Since the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina at its session on the 25th of December, 1991, submitted a request for the international recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the answer came very soon, on the 10th of January, 1992. The commission to which this letter was addressed drafted its opinion number 4 on the 11 January 1992, and it established that Bosnia-Herzegovina met all the requirements for the republics that sought international recognition. The constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina guaranteed the rights of all its national groups, national minorities, and the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina gave the guarantees that they did not have any pretensions to any -- any aspirations towards the neighbouring states. The commission was of the opinion that Bosnia and Herzegovina met the conditions for international recognition. However, since one day before the Serbian republic was proclaimed as a -- as a state within the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the commission was of the opinion that this decision should be tested at a referendum. This referendum was held on the 29th of February and 1st of March, 1992, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. At this referendum, over 60 per cent of the total population voted in favour of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehic, when was Bosnia and Herzegovina recognised as an independent state?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: It was on the 6th of April, 1992 that Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised by the European Union. And on the following day, on the 7th of April, 1992, it was recognised by the United States of America. The decision that was adopted by the European Union on the 6th of April was moved to the 7th of April. So one can consider this to be the day of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina since there is still associations present, and that the 6th of April there was an attack on Yugoslavia during the Second World War. And for that reason, the decision that was adopted on the 6th of April was pushed forward to the 7th of April, and this is now the day of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document 0378 and the first document under D bearing the number 0385, and can you please tell me whether these are the opinions of the Badinter Commission that you just mentioned or -- and the document that served to recognise Bosnia, which was drafted in Luxembourg on the 6th of April, 1991? Have you been able to find these two documents? That's the last document under C and the first document under D.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: I have an opinion of the commission dated 11 January 1992, the opinion number 4. And document under D is the declaration on proclaiming Bosnia and Herzegovina an independent state, and the date on this document is the 6th of April, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Dr. Sehic, in your expert report, in pages from 37 to 51, you give the basic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to remind you that you have an hour and a half theoretically, so in about five minutes you should bring your examination-in-chief to an end.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you have decided that we have an hour and a half. I'll try to speed up, but I cannot complete my examination-in-chief in five minutes. I will probably need 15 to 20 minutes. May I be granted 15 or 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you may be granted that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sehic, on pages from 37 to 51 of your report, you have given us an overview of the military and political developments in the years 1992 and 1993. Can you please tell us very briefly what are the characteristics of the year 1992, after the 6th of April of that year, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: After the 6th of April, 1992, the military operation started in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Yugoslav army started participating in those events. During the month of April and May, its -- it would be organised, and it would become the army of the Serbian republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina. A series of military operations that involved paramilitaries led to the occupation of the large part of the country, some 70 out of the per cent of the country was occupied. The 30 per cent was the area of Central Bosnia and the area around Bihac. However, during the first onslaught, the entire area of Eastern Bosnia came under the occupation. A series of resolutions and decisions passed by the United Nations and the international institutions implicate the army in those events, and that is why they passed a certain number of resolutions in 1992 which blamed the military bodies and the political bodies in Belgrade. That's why in the course of 1992 a lot of resolutions were adopted introducing sanctions against Serbia and the former Yugoslavia. As far as the other political events in Bosnia and Herzegovina are concerned, there were still two options immediately after the break-out of the war in 1992. Since this area, as we have already said, was proclaimed the Croatian autonomous region, this led to the establishment of the Croatian state of Herceg-Bosna, which was another paramilitary state which had all the characteristics of the SAO [as interpreted]. However, it was never legalised and recognised. On the 14th of September, the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed this formation to be illegal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sehic, from this part can you please answer just one question. You have already discussed the issue of the international diplomacy. Bosnia and Herzegovina was proclaimed independent and became a member of the United Nations. Can you please tell me, what measures were put in place by the international community in order to help their member to protect its independent and territorial integrity?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Since Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the 22nd of May, 1992, became a member of the United Nations, according to the United Nations Charter, the United Nations were duty-bound to provide all forms of assistance to its member. However, this was not the case in the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was Bosnia and Herzegovina in a position to help itself? Were there any instruments in place, put in place by the international community that restricted their ability to help themselves?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such instruments. I believe that Bosnia and Herzegovina was punished by the decision that was adopted in 1991 by which an embargo was put on the import of arms. First and foremost, the Yugoslav People's Army was very well-armed. It was the third- or fourth-ranking military force in the territory of the Balkan Peninsula. Bosnia and Herzegovina remained unarmed, unprotected, and all the assistance that it received boiled down to humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at map 14 and tell me, please, whether it represents the formation that you have just mentioned that was known as the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a map of Herceg-Bosna, which encompasses 30 districts, and according to the structure, to a large extent this very much reflects the territory of the Croatian banovina from the year 1939.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sehic, towards the end of 1992 and in 1993, did the international community try in other ways to solve the problem of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina? How did these initiatives end?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992 and the -- already in the second half of 1992, there was the so-called Geneva conference which would led to some results at the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993. The result of all that was the Vance-Owen Plan which was drafted in 1993 of that year. This document bring about major changes and would have impact on the developments which would take place in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and especially in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us why was this document very important? Why did it have such major consequences?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Plan which was published on the 2nd of January, 1993, involved four documents that were success civil signed between January and March 1993. The main reason why this plan was important was as follows: According to the agreement, the signing of all the parts of the Vance-Owen Plan would put this plan in effect. However, what happened was that Croats signed all the parts of this peace plan during the months of January and February. The Muslims signed all these documents in January, February, and March. However, the Serbian republic never signed this peace plan. First they refused to sign it on the 2nd of April in Bileca, and then on the 26th of April. So this plan effectively never took off the ground and was never put in effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There have been many exhibits brought before this Tribunal about Bosnia and Herzegovina, the HVO, and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Could you please tell us based on the documents you had at your disposal, what was the approach to the implementation of this plan which was carried out by Bosnia or the Croatian part of it?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: In this documentary part, there were several documents which point to the way. When we're talking about the Vance-Owen Plan and its influence on the political and military events, I believe that two documents are crucial here. The first one is from the 15th of January, 1993, and that is from a meeting which was held in Mostar, which provided under five or six items for the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan. Although there was no definitive agreement and this wasn't signed, the implementation began unilaterally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please just tell us who held this meeting.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: The meeting was held by the military and political leadership of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: After the meeting, the differences between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council became greater and became even more sharp following a meeting in Mostar on the 3rd of April, 1993, when an ultimatum was practically given to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina that it should withdraw from provinces which according to the Vance-Owen Plan were to be given to the Croatian component, which meant that the plan was supposed to be realised even before the peace process was completed and the entire contract was signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sehic, could you please look at map 15 now and tell us what it depicts.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: You can see the Vance-Owen Plan on the map and the distribution or the division into ten provinces. On this map, you can see what this division was like. The Muslims were given provinces 1, 5, and 9. The Croats were awarded 8 and 10 and 3. And then 2, 4, and 6 were given to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you said that the plan never went into effect, and you also testified that it resulted in major consequences following the ultimatum to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, could you please tell us whether international diplomacy tried to resolve this question in a different way, and whether by the end of 1993 or early 1994 a solution was found which stopped the conflict between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: In mid-1993 and in late 1993, so by the end of the year, what was symptomatic for the relationship at the time were actual -- several plans of which I would just mention after the Vance-Owen Plan fell through, which was insisted upon until June. During June and July, afterwards different plans became current. For example, the Stoltenberg plan from August 1993, which would be finalised only actually in late 1993 and early 1994. However, a more active engagement by the United States in the course of 1994 has -- brought about a major turnaround. Prompted by the American initiative, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established. The conflicts would stop, and in a certain way it could be said that with the establishment of the federation, major problems were solved which had been topical throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I'm primarily thinking of the conflict between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at map 16 and 17 and tell us what they show.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: On map 16 you can see the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan which was presented in August 1993. This plan to a certain extent deviated from the Vance-Owen Plan, and the reasons for that are probably known to the participants themselves, because in 1993 and 1994, agreements were reached on the ratios of certain provinces. And it can be then assumed with some degree of certainty that the role of the military operations played a role in these -- in the distribution of these territories. According to the plan, the Croats would receive 25.6 per cent of the plan. This was under the Vance-Owen Plan. Under the Stoltenberg Plan this figure was actually 17.5. While Muslims were given 26 per cent of the Vance-Owen Plan under the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan this became 28 per cent, and then by the end of the year it actually became 33 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sehic, at the beginning you said it was practically impossible to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina according to the ethnic principle, and you showed us many plans by the international community that was trying to help solve the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could you please tell us what the main disadvantages of these plans were?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Since I dealt with international diplomacy in a little more detail, I can say that the relationships between the great powers had an effect on these plans. Their mutual relations led to the fact that there wasn't too much consistency in implementing the principles which had been adopted as early as 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you now look at map 17, which I would like to show you, and tell us what that depicts.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Map 17 shows the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the formation of which was to a great degree the result of the activities of the United States, who effected the conciliation of the two opposing sides in the course of 1994, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO. And with the signing of the Washington Agreement, the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established, also providing for the rest of the country, meaning the Serbian part, would become a part of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which can be concluded on the basis of the constitution under which the federation, the republic would be entrusted with the defence and economic functions. The functions would be divided into federation and state authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to the cultural heritage of the country, could you please tell us why was it so important to treat this issue in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Never throughout its history spanning more than a thousand years Bosnia-Herzegovina did not experience such a level of devastation and destruction of cultural monuments as it did in this war. All the cultural monuments attested to the long history and the presence of its -- of Bosnia and the presence of its inhabitants in this territory. In this war, there were attempts in a certain way to erase the roots of others, to cleanse the territory, and to remove traces of the existence of other peoples.
