In my expert report, I dealt a little bit more with the question of the treatment and the relationship of the -- or the position of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Muslim population towards the cultural heritage and the monuments of others. Throughout their history, Muslims never destroyed religious buildings. They actually took part in the building of such buildings. And this was a sign of their desire to share their lives with other people, people of other faiths. Based on documents which were attached and which were available to me, I provided an expert report drafted by expert Collins, which was made for the UNESCO commission in 1995. This question is actually one of the key questions when we're talking about Bosnia and Herzegovina and its attitude towards cultural monuments and cultural heritage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned at the end of your analysis a very important question, the question of ethnic cleansing and the relocation of the population, which was in early 1991 was mixed throughout the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you please tell me why you thought it was important to deal with this particular segment in a historical context dealing with the history of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: I think it is important because it indicates that Bosnia and Herzegovina never in its long history had ethnically or religiously defined territories. If this did happen sometime in its history, it could have been just a result of some violent events, and it would be counter to any historical principles. When we're talking about ethnic cleansing, which is a euphemism for genocide, it's a different word for genocide, I believe that this idea is an anachronous to this time, but it had a very important role in all the events in 1992, 1993, and 1994. Numerous documents that I reviewed led me to emphasise several. One would be a study or an analysis which would be given to representatives of the United Nations and UNESCO. Also, this is an analysis which deals with the main facts and the main intentions underlying ethnic cleansing in a particular territory, particularly the territory of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, Dr. Sehic, as a researcher who has been studying the history of Bosnia and Herzegovina for a long time, a professional person, could you please draw parallels between some tendencies in more recent and more removed history and the events between 1992 and 1995 in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: It's possible to draw some historical parallels. I believe that the closest thing to the events from 1992 to 1995 was something that had existed and was established in the period from 1939, just prior to the outbreak of World War II. That was the establishment of the banovina of Croatia, the project of Serbian lands, the struggle of Muslims for autonomy of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I believe that these projects, these historical projects, had been revived in the course of the war from 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have finished with the examination-in-chief of our expert. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. Residovic. The other Defence team representing General Kubura, do they wish to put any questions to the expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We do not have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm going to turn to the Prosecution and give them the floor for their cross-examination of the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President; good afternoon to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor. In response to my -- can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In response to questions from my colleague, you stated that this area that you dealt with is not, and I quote you, "My field of strict academic interest." Bearing in mind that you have admitted that this area is not in your field of strict academic interest, would you agree with me then if I said that some of the suggestions made in the report may not be accurate or reliable?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: I would like to hear those suggestions and then I could give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's first start with the list. You indicated to us that you looked at a list of documents presented to you by the Defence in arriving at some of your conclusions, but have you indicated in your annexes these lists and where these sources were derived from?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Each source has been given. I have provided the source of each document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So I take it that you have provided a list with documents or excerpts from the Celebici case that you quoted. Is that on the list?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you, in drafting the report, consult Croatian documents such as presidential transcripts, which is exhibited at the ICTY and which is in the public domain? Did you use documents such as those in the drafting of your report?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Such documents were not made available to me, and I did not have access to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What of the perhaps BH leadership material such as Presidency minutes, assembly transcripts? Did you consider these in the drafting of the report?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes, a part of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, I wish to talk a little bit about the population distribution, because you did touch quite a bit on it, and my question to you is: Would I be correct in saying that the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina had the least advantage of the population distribution?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I already said that in my report. And I looked at that, and I analysed 1991, the results of the last population census. A greater concentration of the Croat population was presented in only one part, because the concentration of the Croat population was in three separate regions. One of them was in Northern Bosnia. The second was in Central Bosnia, and the third area with such a concentration was Herzegovina. In studies or when you analyse this, what you can see when you look at the structure of the population in 1991, you can see that the Muslims had the highest concentration of the populations up to 82 per cent. The concentration of the Serb population went up to 62 per cent, while the concentration of the Croat population was below 50 per cent, around 45 per cent. An unfavourable fact for the distribution of the Croat population was primarily when you looked at this region where they did have a majority, and I mentioned four reasons for this in my expert report, that these were the most economically backward areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the most sparsely populated areas, especially the region of Herzegovina. I also mentioned several other points. There were no economic or political centres in these areas. And the fourth and last fact that I mentioned in this context was the fact that all the important cultural monuments of the Croats were outside of the areas where the Croat population had a majority. And these four reasons which I mentioned lead us to conclude that the Croat population was in a least favourable position according to the results of the census from 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And in a nutshell, overall the Muslims were in the majority. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to the census from 1991, the Muslims had -- helped over 43 per cent of the population. And this kept growing. And according to the last two censuses of the population, first of all they came to represent more than 50 per cent of the overall population of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992, how would you describe the -- the Croatian army's relationship with the BH army? In the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: This question isn't quite clear. What do you mean by the relationship between the Croatian army and the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe I could put it a different way. Was the Croatian army during that period, spring of 1992, welcome in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992, there was no military activity in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, later on, after an armed conflict broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the situation changed. As far as the Croatian army is concerned, there was a UN resolution adopted on the 18th of May, 1992, according to which the military forces, the JNA and the Croatian army, were to withdraw from Bosnia and Herzegovina or to place themselves under the control of the official organs of power in Bosnia and Herzegovina, namely the Presidency. As far as the question as to whether their presence, the presence of the Croatian army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was welcome is concerned, well, this has to do with international relations, relations between two states. Any assistance offered to the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to preserve this state would have been welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Wasn't the Croatian army perceived as fighting against the aggressor, which was the Serbs at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Well, one might have considered that in a certain sense the Croatian army, as of April 1992, was involved in activities in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If we remember the fact that various military formations were established, for example, the Croatian Armed Forces which were active in Herceg -- Herzegovina in particular, and to an extent in Bosnia as well, above all in Zenica, these were, after all, military forces from Bosnia and Herzegovina. But the question as to what the meaning of the presence of the Croatian army in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina meant is a different question because these were armies that came from two states that had obtained international recognition.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm wrong, but at one point in time somewhere in the spring of 1992, there was an attempt by both armies to put up one solid front. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what they attempted to do. I think that a number of agreements were first signed at the political level between President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic, that is between Bosnia and Croatia. Agreements were signed on a number of occasions and these agreements stated that the Republic of Croatia would support the efforts made by Bosnia and Herzegovina to resist the aggression committed against it. They also stated that Croatia would continue to provide Bosnia and Herzegovina with aid. Such agreements were signed on a number of occasions. On the 16th of June, 1992, for the first time, and then on the 21st of July, 1992, and finally on the 23rd of September, 1992, in New York. As far as this question is concerned, as far as the involvement of the Croatian army in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned, this is an issue that should have been agreed on at the level of state.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So, then, would I be correct if I conclude that the relationship, so to speak, for want of a better word, did not materialise because the Muslim leaders would respect all the agreements that you have spoken about here today? The Muslim leaders are the ones who refused to join, who refused to sign?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that would be a one-sided interpretation of such an agreement between states. There was an agreement on cooperation, but as for signing a military agreement between two independent states is concerned, this is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, maybe we could sort of get it clarified. Page 35 of your report, and that's English version, at the bottom of the page it says: "Croatian influence on the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina was increasingly apparent." I am not sure. Maybe my friends can help you with respect to the -- it's page 35, the last paragraph. That's the English version. It's under "The military and political situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina," and it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to assist you, it's on page 44 of the Bosnian version, and it's in paragraph 2. "Croatian influence on the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina was increasingly apparent."

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Have you seen it? "Croatian influence on the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina was increasingly apparent --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And you went on to explain. But could you explain for us or clarify what you mean by this, and on what basis was this statement made?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: This part of the report deals with the events in June and July 1992. When I spoke about this awhile ago, when I spoke about the joint signing of agreements on cooperation between President Izetbegovic and President Tudjman, I said that among other items in the agreement, there was an item concerning all forms of assistance. However, in -- earlier on in the report, I raised an issue that concerned the involvement of the Croatian army, the Croatian army which came to Bosnia and Herzegovina without the legal Bosnian and Herzegovinian organs of power being aware of this fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I'm going to have to seek some guidance from my friend. It's page 33 of the English version, and it's footnote 76.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 41 in the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Have you -- have you found it? Have you found it? Have you found it? Could you explain? This is --

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and first could you explain the -- the source or the basis on which this -- this note was written?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: As far as footnote 76 is concerned, it relates to an explanation on organisation of military units that were described as Muslim ones. I mentioned the fact that this was not new. I provided a number of examples since I'd been particularly involved in military history and especially Austro-Hungarian military history. In such an organisation when including Muslim inhabitants in the army of Austria and Hungary, which was a Christian one, in such organisations the traditions and beliefs of the Muslim people were respected. As stated here, they were given religious freedom and their religious rights and customs were fully respected. This was not just with respect to the Austro-Hungarian period. This is also something that existed in the state of Yugoslavia after 1918 and between the two wars, these customs and the religious rights of Muslims and the religious needs of Muslims were fully respected, and this was provided for in the laws. In the course of the Second World War, this tradition was also respected, and on a number of occasions a number of partisan units were established which were called Muslim partisan units. Even brigades and battalions were organised. For example, the 16th Muslim Brigade, which was one of the largest units. And there was an entire series of partisan units which were described as Muslim ones. In the -- in socialist Yugoslavia, this tradition continued. It continued right up until the break-up of Yugoslavia. And reference is made to all these facts in footnote number 76. I can say that on the whole this is the result of research and the result of an analysis of numerous documents that I also made use of when preparing my doctoral thesis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And if I understood you clearly, are you saying that this 7th Muslim Brigade was merely an attempt to accommodate the religious needs of the Muslims, or are you saying that that brigade was formulated based on the -- on the needs of Muslims, to accommodate the religious needs of Muslims or -- was that what the 7th Muslim Brigade was all about?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: I've only been referring to the principles on which the basis of which units were formed. These principles involved respect for religious freedom. It's above all necessary to be aware of the fact that only after 1945 these traditions were no longer respected. One no longer took into consideration the specific nature of people or the religions of people in the JNA. No attention was paid to the food provided to different people, people of different religions, because above all, this army was an atheist army, and this religious freedom was curtailed. And for 45 years all national characteristics were suppressed. So I think that this could be a reaction to units being established on these principles. This was a long term process.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So then would I be correct in assuming or saying that the 7th Muslim Brigade accommodated the Muslim race, so that your foreigners who might have been Muslims, they automatically would have gone to the 7th Muslim Brigade? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: I think that would be a simplistic interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But according to your theory and according to footnote 76, they tried to accommodate the religious practices, in this instance the Muslim practice, and so that was inculcated into the 7th Muslim Brigade. So based on your theory, am I right in concluding that members of the Muslim faith who wanted to join the army, so to speak, the BiH army, the Muslims would naturally be channeled to the 7th Muslim Brigade? Based on their religious practices, of course.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say so. Since they insisted, if religion played a role, if it played a significant role, it doesn't necessarily mean that they would have to join that brigade alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't necessarily mean that they would have to join that brigade alone, but it necessarily means that that might be the most appropriate brigade for them to join based on their religion?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that it wasn't the only unit in which religious traditions, religious practice was respected. I don't think only the 7th Muslim Brigade did this. This was a tradition widespread among the Muslim population. They would celebrate religious festivities, perform religious rites, their religious duties. I don't think this could be interpreted in a simple manner. There are certain prejudices that are also present. So those were religious customs like go to the church to play. But I think there are a lot of prejudices in relation to this act.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Let's move on. Could you explain for the Trial Chamber exactly what was the Celebici agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: The Celebici agreement on the 16th of June, 1993, is only briefly referred to in the report. This is an agreement that the media, the international media relayed. This states that there was an agreement reached between the Serbs and Croats on humanitarian relocation of the population. You can see that I quoted from the French newspaper Le Figaro, and the newspaper states that this agreement on cleansing the population was reached.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: If I were to say to you that based on what you had earlier said about this area not being your field of strict academic interests, coupled with the fact that you have indicated in the report on June 16, 1993, almost all the media cited this Celebici agreement, yet you have only quoted one, the French newspaper. If I were to say to you that this statement here in the report, like many other statements, are not -- is not entirely accurate, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: As far as media reports are concerned, most of the reports paid a lot of attention to the Celebici agreement, the agreement on the humanitarian relocation of the population. To gain a clear idea of this, there is another report that the president of Croatia, Tudjman, provided in 1995. He is also quoted here. And this report mentions the idea of the humanitarian relocation of the population. And as Tudjman states in his interview, the first agreements on this matter were reached within the framework of the Geneva conference. The first agreements on the humanitarian relocation of the population were reached. And he explained how this exchange of the population should be implemented. And he also mentioned the reasons for which this was to be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Anto Valenta, as referred to in the report just a couple lines below the Celebici agreement, because it deals with him, and you refer to him as the HB -- HZ HB vice-president. Now, would you agree with me if I say that your facts are wrong and if I tell you from research Anto Valenta was merely an HVO vice-president and that and Kordic was the HZ HB vice-president? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: The report says the vice-president, the deputy president. The meaning is the same. That was the term used. It's the terms that the Croats used, Dopredsjednik instead of Potpredsjednik. Both terms mean vice-president.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Is -- well, correct me if I'm wrong, but maybe my research was wrong, too, but isn't the HVO vice-president different from the HZ HB vice-president? Isn't it two different roles?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: I think on the 10th of May when this letter was sent to Anto Valenta, I think he was the vice-president of the HZ HB, not the vice-president of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And you say, "I think," which gives the impression that you're not sure.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: If this is what I wrote, well, perhaps I could have made a mistake, but I can immediately check this in the relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Can I -- can I suggest to you, then, that there may have been quite a few more errors like this one in this report during the period 1990 to 1995, especially, especially since it is not your - sorry - especially since it's not your field of academic interest? Is there a possibility that there is room for more errors in the report? Did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think that there are errors. Maybe there is a typo. But if you are implying that my report is not professional, I can assure you that I have published a number of papers on the years 1992 and 1993. My research took quite a long time while I was staying in the Republic of Germany, and I consider myself fully competent to provide an opinion on this period in the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have all the necessary documents, and if there is an error such as you imply there is, I don't think you're right. I believe that there are no errors in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Contrary to the fact, and my apologies, it was not meant to mean that the report was not a professional one. My -- my statement and which I ask you to agree with or not to agree with was the fact that you yourself indicated to the Trial Chamber that this area is not your area. This is not your field. And I'm saying in light of that, if it is possible that there could be inaccuracies in the report, if there is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, when I was talking about this report, I based my words on the period that I'm involved in, and that is the period of Austro-Hungarian, and I have a Ph.D in that period. However, my field of expertise is the politics of the 20th century, and the object of my research is the period after the break-up of Yugoslavia and events which took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina between the period 1992 and 1995. Since I'm very much involved in the topic of world history, this is my strict field of expertise, the events which have taken place after the year of 1918 until the present, and I believe that I'm fully competent to provide an expert opinion on this period of history.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, this concludes the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is twenty-five to six. We are going to make another break, and we shall resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Benjamin, do you have any other questions at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence teams. After the cross-examination by the Prosecution, do you have any re-examination for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We do not have any additional questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have a few questions to put to you which arise from a question that the Prosecution has put to you regarding the problems with religion. You have indicated in your expert report, on page -- you have made a reference in footnote 76 to the question of the Muslim unity, and you have indicated in that footnote that in 1941, the Muslims joined the Partisans and -- and that there were units which were created at the time, and you quoted 7th Muslim Brigade, which was established in Tuzla. And you also indicate in that footnote that the Muslims joined such units, such Partisan units because that had to do with their future in Yugoslavia. In the Socialist Federative State of Yugoslavia, after the year 1945 in the Yugoslav army, were there in the army any religious feelings or did the socialist ideology completely curb the religious feelings, and it was no longer a topical issue, the -- you as an expert witness, what can you tell us about that issue?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: The traditions that existed before that time, after the establishment of the Yugoslav state in 1945, was suppressed. After that time, it was the ideology that dominated. All the religious symbols were suppressed because the state was an atheist state. Any form of religious symbols in the Yugoslav People's Army were banned. As for the specific features that existed before, they were simply erased. These specific characteristics were respected before that time for a long period of time. After the year 1945, this was no longer the case. Since I myself served in this army, I can tell you that one of the problems was diet. It was a well-known fact that people observing Muslim religion do not eat pork. However, in the Yugoslav People's Army, they were forced to eat pork. There was no choice for them. They could either eat or go hungry. So it was the ideology that came first, and religion was completely separated from both the state and its army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood you correctly, the ideology in the former Yugoslavia was such that any distinctive religious signs were not to be evident in -- in the army. You yourself said that you served in the JNA. You provided a number of examples. Following your analysis, would one say that when Bosnia and Herzegovina became a state, religious feelings rapidly reappeared and were given much importance given the decades that had passed during which it was impossible to establish religious feelings. Do you see a causal relation between the fact that the BH army had units of that kind at the time? Last week we had a witness who was involved in moral and religious affairs. Do you see a causal relationship in these matters?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that there is a causal relationship between the suppression of something. In this case this was tradition, especially when it came to religious symbols. For a long period of time, lasting for almost a half a century, there was a significant influence that appeared after the year 1992. Again there was a comeback to the principles and origins of religion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now onto another subject. It has been indicated to us that the movement was established based on ethnic principles. I'm talking about the Serbian republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The question of Croats again has been pointed out to us, and in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state which consisted of Muslims. Between the ideology that was a socialist ideology and the national feeling, was there a disparity between nationalist feeling because of the presence of an ideology, or a state, as you have indicated, which was atheist but at the same time of a state where the nationalist feelings had not been curbed? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: As far as the nationalist ideologies in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina are concerned, one would have to go back into the second half of the 19th century and speak about the significance of the process of the growth and development of nations in the territory of the Balkans and the east -- south-eastern Europe. The main ideas which were present at the time in Europe, especially Herder's Europe, one people, one state, were being built into all the national programs of the Balkan states. This was particularly typical of the second half of the 19th century. The nationalist movements that existed in the south-eastern Europe, especially in Bosnia-Herzegovina, those were the nationalist movements of the neighbouring states of Serbia and Croatia. These nationalist movements moved to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the 60s and the 70s of the 19th century, and they culminated in the second half of the 19th century, and particularly towards the end of the 19th century. During the Austro-Hungarian administration, these state -- states saw liberalisation of attitude towards religion, towards national issues, the establishment of schools, national symbols, and from the 90s onwards, the fight for national and religious autonomy started in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This fight ended before the 1910, at the moment when the Austro-Hungarian administration, to a certain extent, provided for the freedom of nationalist and religious feelings and the establishment of these movements in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Later on, when we're talking about the relationships between ethnic groups, between the two wars one could notice two concepts. There was a nationalist Serbian movement and a nationalist Croatian movement. Between the two of them, there were Bosnian-Herzegovinian Muslims who still had their nationalist ideology within their religion. After the Second World War, one could say that to a certain extent in 1949, after the abolishment of all ethnic organisations, alliances, and particularly those that were of a religion -- religious nature, the ideology of the ruling system prevailed so that nationalist symbols became suppressed. The Yugoslav idea prevailed at the time, and this would be the case all the way up to the death of Josip Broz Tito. In a certain way, ethnic symbols were suppressed, and after the death of Josip Broz Tito, the general crisis that prevailed in the crisis will lead to the conditions being put in place for the surge of nationalistic feelings. This started, as I've already explained, not in the peripheral parts of Yugoslavia but, rather, in its core, in Serbia. The process that started in 1986 culminated in 1992 with the developments that took place at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that information. I'll move on to another subject now. Could you have a look at map number 15 and at map number 16 too. Map 15 is -- represents the Vance-Owen Plan, and map number 16 represents the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. Will you have a look at the map. If you compare the two maps, one can see that Travnik and Bugojno, which in the Stoltenberg Plan are attached to Bosnia-Herzegovina, you can see that these places in the Owen plan, these places Travnik and Bugojno were attached to the Croatian entity. So one notes that when comparing these two plans that in the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan the Bugojno and Travnik zone is placed within the zone, the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslim area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. How do we explain the fact that this was done given that the document, the census from 1991 which you provided us with, which is a list of municipalities and the population, we can see in this list that in Bugojno the Bosniak population was 1961 -- the Croats were 1.600, the Serbs 8.000, and the others 2.004. We notice that Bugojno didn't have a Muslim majority. And similarly in Travnik, the situation is the same. Since there were 31.813 Bosniak -- Bosniaks, 26.000 Croats, and 7.000 Serbs. So these areas weren't Muslim -- inhabited by Muslim majority. So how do you explain the fact that the situation has changed in the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan? These places are then placed within a Muslim zone. Could you explain this?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: As you can see in the Vance-Owen Plan, Travnik and Bugojno were integrated in the Croatian provinces as had been planned by the Vance-Owen Plan. The second plan, which is the topic of our discussion here today, is the so-called Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, which followed some eight and a half months after the first maps of the Vance-Owen Plan were presented. During that period, between January and October, there some military populations took place, and the explanation could be that the changes were impacted by the fact that, for example, in the month of August when the Stoltenberg plan was adopted, these towns, Bugojno and Travnik, were under the control of the units of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So as a witness expert, you say that in fact this plan took into consideration the presence of BH forces in this area. This is what would explain the plan. By following this reasoning, if they had got as far as Jajce or Kupres, in such case perhaps the plan would have in some way confirmed the military action. Is that your interpretation? The plan, the Stoltenberg-Owen Plan, in fact, confirmed the situation such as it was in military terms. I have another question to provide you with, to ask you. In the binder that Defence counsel provided you with, document 520, this is a statement made by Colonel Kordic, and Colonel Kordic says the following when taking the oath: "The Croatian territory of Zenica is Croatian." How can he say such a thing given that when we have a look at the 1991 census we can see that in Zenica there are 80.000 -- over 80.000 Bosniaks and there are only 22.000 Croats? How can one affirm that Zenica is Croat, since according to the census the situation is the contrary? How could you explain such a statement?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the explanation would be as follows: Obviously since the population in Zenica -- most of the population in Zenica was of Muslim ethnic group and Croats were a minority, how can one account for such words? One would have to go a bit back in the history. During the month of March 1992, within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, an issue was raised. The issue was as to what would happen with the territories where Muslims had a majority and how should Croats organise themselves in those areas? I believe this is a document from the 17th of March, and it was concluded that in the territory of Zenica there should be a part where Croats constituted a majority, and this part should be separated from the rest of Zenica. The HVO or HVO units were to be established in the territory of Zenica as a special army unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you interpret this statement as the HVO desire to separate the Zenica area, to divide it into two parts depending on the presence of Muslim inhabitants or Croatian inhabitants. That's how you interpret this statement. The last subject I want to address, on page 39 of your report, you mention the Jeddah Islamic conference. Ministers of foreign affairs from Arab countries were concerned and you said that Lord Owen attended this conference, and you said that on that occasion, the subject of lifting the embargo on weapons was raised, and the co-presidents of the conference, Lord Owen and Mr. Vance, were against lifting the embargo but I quote, you said, "The participants in the conference did not exclude the possibility of having recourse to military force pursuant to Article 42 of the UN Charter." According to the research that you carried out, according to your studies, did you gain the impression that in spite of Lord Owen's and Mr. Vance's participation they might have sidestepped the embargo on arms and may have provided weapons to troops in Bosnia-Herzegovina. What were the conclusions that you reached when carrying out your research?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, looking at the documents that I used in preparing my report, I can say that I've used documents from a magazine or a journal which is considered to be one of the most significant European magazines covering international politics. The document reflects the facts that are contained in my report, and the question itself whether the Arabic countries might have been prompted to lift the embargo of their own accord and deliver arms to Bosnia and Herzegovina, one would have to have in mind the issue of the implementation of such a decision even if it had been made. All the routes to Bosnia were blocked, and it would have been very difficult to implement such a decision. And even if such a decision had been made, it would have been pointless if at the same time routes had not been provided for the delivery of arms. Bearing in mind the conditions that prevailed in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the total encirclement of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this was completely out of the question and impossible to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does the Prosecution or the Defence have any questions that arise from the Chamber's questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have only two questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Sehic, the president of the Trial Chamber showed you the Vance-Owen map and the Stoltenberg map. With regard to these maps, I would like to ask you the following: The ethnic principle which appeared in all the peace plans as the basis for the plan, to what extent did it correspond to the essence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to what extent did it in fact provoke nationalist desires to break up Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: We would need to go back a little bit and start from the beginning of 1990 to see which principles should have been used to establish these negotiations and to seek principles for the founding of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The international community had several proposals. The decision of the commission of the 24th of December, whose president was the chairman of the commission court, Mr. Robert Badinter, had those principles been adopted, war might not have broken out. As far as the ethnic principles are concerned, throughout the entire period at all of these international negotiations, we had the first peace plan. That was the Cutileiro plan. Then two meetings which followed in Lisbon. That agreement lost its significance once the war broke out. But all the plans were important, beginning from the Vance-Owen Plan, then the Stoltenberg Plan, and all of them were based on this ethnic principle. As far as the ethnic principle is concerned, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina constantly refused divisions and the reaching of an agreement should the principles in order to reach a peace agreement be based solely on ethnic principles. As early as June 1992, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted a platform which stayed in force throughout the whole war, and they stood by all of those principles mentioned in the platform to ensure all the people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and national minorities enjoyed equal rights. All of these peace treaties and these peace plans are counter to the essence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a matter of fact. This is an attempt at divisions based on ethnic lines, although the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina always lived intermingled. And if you see the map of 1991, you can see, and it was something that was always said, that the map looked like a leopard skin because all the population was intermingled.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Does the Prosecution have any questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... two.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: If you had the opportunity to look at other sources, example, the Croatian documents exhibited by the ICTY, could you say whether your conclusion that arrived at in your report could have been different?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD SEHIC
utterances.text: I have already said which sources I used. I've already said that besides using the reference materials for this historical period I also used documents which were provided to me by the Defence, primarily documents of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, followed by documents of the Croatian Defence Council. Also, the case materials from cases that have already been completed such as the Celebici, Blaskic, and Kordic cases. So it's a question of whether new documents would change my opinion. I believe that they would not. Each document I analysed using the comparative method, and I, on that basis, established its validity. I did not rely on drawing conclusions based on unilateral interpretations because this happens if you only use one historical source. I used various literature, various documents from the Bosnian army, the Croatian side, and I also used some documents from international institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Sehic, this concludes your testimony as an expert witness. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for all the answers you provided put to you by Defence counsel, the Prosecution, and the Chamber. Naturally we wish you all the best in your career as a lecturer, and we wish you a good trip home. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now turn to the Prosecution to deal with the tendering into evidence the annex documents, documents relating to the report and the documents in your binder. You said that these documents were excerpts from other documents. What are you requesting with regard to these documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 72, line 19, I think there is a -- a slip of the tongue. I think you were addressing the Defence. So I would like to respond to what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was referring to the Defence. I was looking at you, so it could only have been you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with regard to this expert, we would first of all like to suggest that his report be admitted into evidence, because I think that when answering questions put to him by all of the parties, including the Chamber, he showed that this report was credible. Therefore, I would like to tender it into evidence. I also want to tender some maps into evidence, the maps from 1 to 17, since this witness confirmed that he himself made a list of these maps and mentioned the sources from which these maps were obtained. As far as the documents are concerned, the documents that we would like to tender into evidence from the numerous documents that we have been provided with by the witness, we don't want to tender into evidence any documents that relate to factual events. Therefore, the Defence will not be suggesting that the documents that concern the BH army be admitted into evidence. We'll do this through witnesses who will be appearing in the future. We will do this for HVO documents as well. We will ask that witnesses confirm these documents, witnesses who have knowledge about these events. Since we only want to tender some of the expert documents into evidence, books, reports, the scientific basis which is an integral part of the entire opus of Dr. Sehic, I'd be grateful if we could compile a list of these documents since we haven't had the time to do so yet. And as usual, we would then tender these documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you are saying that at this moment you are preparing a list of all the documents, but there will be the expert report, the 17 maps, and documents that you will select. But you are not prepared at the moment, so you will inform us of the documents you want to tender into evidence tomorrow or the day after tomorrow. So it is not necessary to ask the Prosecution for their comments since we do not have the list of all the documents yet. We will deal with this issue tomorrow or the day after tomorrow. As far as the witnesses scheduled for the future proceedings, what could you inform us of?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we move into private session now, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of November, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
